hints: Look carefully at the shape of the graph in Fig. 3.2 - in A the mass of DNA per nucleus stays flat at $0.08 \, pg$, while in B it rises steadily to $0.16 \, pg$. Think about what that tells you about whether new DNA is being made.

Recall the order of interphase: first a gap phase with normal metabolic activity, then the synthesis phase where DNA is replicated, then a second gap. Match the flat line and the rising line to those jobs.
walkthrough:
Read the DNA mass as a clue to activity**
In stage A the mass stays constant at $0.08 \, pg$ per nucleus. No extra DNA is being made, so the cell is carrying out normal growth and protein synthesis. This is the first gap of interphase, G1.

Link the rise in DNA to replication**
In stage B the mass rises from $0.08 \, pg$ to $0.16 \, pg$ - it exactly doubles. That doubling is DNA replication, where each chromosome is copied to form two sister chromatids. This defines the S phase, for synthesis of DNA.
Final answer: A - G1 / first gap phase; B - S / synthesis phase (DNA replication).

hints: In D the DNA mass per nucleus falls from $0.16 \, pg$ back to $0.08 \, pg$ before cytokinesis happens. Think about which mitotic stage creates two separate nuclei, so each new nucleus gets half the DNA.
walkthrough:
Why D must be the end of mitosis**
Stage C is the flat top at $0.16 \, pg$ - the cell still has one nucleus containing doubled DNA. In D the value per nucleus drops sharply back to $0.08 \, pg$. That can only happen if one nucleus has divided into two, so each gets one set of chromatids. Nuclear division is completed in telophase, just before the cytoplasm divides in cytokinesis.

hints: Picture the end of mitosis in an animal cell - the two groups of chromosomes have reached opposite poles. What must be rebuilt around each group to make two proper nuclei?
Think about tidying up for division of the whole cell - what happens to the spindle, and how are the cytoplasm and organelles prepared to be shared between the two daughter cells?
walkthrough:
Rebuilding two nuclei**
After sister chromatids separate, a nuclear envelope reforms around each group of chromosomes at opposite poles. That creates two separate nuclei within the one cell, each with its own membrane.

Preparing the cytoplasm to split**
At the same time the spindle that pulled chromatids apart breaks down and disappears. Organelles made during interphase are distributed so both ends of the cell will receive a share, and in an animal cell a cleavage furrow starts to pinch in, formed by a contractile ring of actin microfilaments under the cell surface membrane. This sets up cytokinesis.

Final answer: Any two: nuclear envelope reforms around each group of chromosomes to form two nuclei; spindle fibres disassemble / disappear; increase in cytoplasm / number of organelles and organelles distributed to be shared; cleavage furrow / contractile ring of actin microfilaments forms.

hints: Count nuclei, not DNA amount - A and B are before nuclear division, while D is after the nucleus has divided but before the cytoplasm has split. How many nuclei will be inside the one stem cell in each case?

Remember mitosis makes genetically identical nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent. Even though DNA doubles in S phase, chromosomes are counted as 12 throughout because replicated chromosomes still count as one until sisters separate.
walkthrough:
Track nuclei through the cycle**
In A (G1) and B (S) nuclear division has not happened yet, so there is still 1 nucleus in the cell. In D (telophase) the nucleus has divided into two but cytokinesis has not yet split the cytoplasm, so the one stem cell temporarily contains 2 nuclei.

Keep chromosome number constant**
Mitosis conserves chromosome number. The parent stem cell has 12 chromosomes. DNA replication in B copies each chromosome into two chromatids but does not create new chromosomes, so the count stays 12. After separation each new nucleus in D also receives 12 chromosomes.
Final answer: Number of nuclei within stem cell: A = 1, B = 1, D = 2; Number of chromosomes in each nucleus: A = 12, B = 12, D = 12.

hints: Follow the white cells labelled stem cell in Fig. 3.3 through three divisions - after each division at least one daughter is still a stem cell. What does that tell you about their ability to keep dividing?
Notice the other daughter in each division becomes a grey differentiated cell. Think about why an animal needs a steady supply of new specialised cells.
Link that supply to the needs of a young growing nematode - building new tissues, replacing old or damaged cells, and providing cells that can specialise.
walkthrough:
Self-renewal keeps the stem pool**
Fig. 3.3 shows asymmetric division. Each stem cell divides by mitosis to give one new stem cell and one cell that will specialise. Because one daughter always remains a stem cell, the stem line can keep dividing repeatedly without running out.

Supplying cells for the body**
The other daughters become differentiated (specialised) cells. This provides new cells for growth of the young nematode as it gets larger.

Replacement and specialisation**
The same supply replaces worn out, dead or damaged cells and allows repair of tissues. By differentiating, stem cell daughters can form the different specialised cell types needed for tissues and organs.

Final answer: Stem cells continue to divide repeatedly by mitosis / self-renew, with at least one daughter remaining a stem cell; to produce cells for growth; for repair of tissues / replacement of old / worn out / dead cells; to differentiate / specialise to form tissues / organs.
